about: What you gather in Rome, and what each set brings back to the Nexus (tools/rome_acts/collections.py).

exempla.name: The exempla
exempla.line: The heroes of Rome stand again by Rome's door in the Nexus.

inscriptions.name: The inscriptions
inscriptions.line: Rome's dedication is cut on its stone in the Nexus.

coins.name: The coins
coins.line: Rome's treasury is back under its stone in the Nexus: seven coins, from bronze to nothing.

masks.name: The masks
masks.line: The ancestors' masks hang in their niches in the Nexus.

voices.name: The voices
voices.line: The voices of Rome's families sing together in the Nexus.

steps.say: QUOI HON... SAKROS ES... RECEI... KALATOREM

Under a black stone in the Comitium, the oldest writing in Rome, running up and down like a plough: whoever harms this place is cursed, it says, and it names a king. Nobody can quite read it any more.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: SI IN IUS VOCAT, ITO. NI IT, ANTESTAMINO. IGITUR EM CAPITO.
The law of Rome on bronze by the Rostra: if a man is summoned to court, he shall go. If he does not go, let a witness be called; then let him be seized. Schoolboys learn it by heart.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: VOTE FOR GAIUS JULIUS POLYBIUS FOR AEDILE: HE BRINGS GOOD BREAD. / SUCCESSUS THE WEAVER LOVES THE INNKEEPER'S SLAVE GIRL. / I AM AMAZED, O WALL, THAT YOU HAVE NOT FALLEN DOWN UNDER SO MUCH WRITING.

Election notices painted in red, scratched over with jokes, insults, love and prices. These very lines turn up on the walls of Pompeii; the walls of Rome say the same. Everyone reads a little, and everyone writes on walls.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: M·AGRIPPA·L·F·COS·TERTIVM·FECIT
Marcus Agrippa, son of Lucius, consul for the third time, made this. Hadrian rebuilt the whole temple, and put Agrippa's name back on it, not his own.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: SENATUS POPULUSQUE ROMANUS DIVO TITO DIVI VESPASIANI F. VESPASIANO AUGUSTO
The Senate and People of Rome, to the deified Titus. Inside the arch, in relief, his soldiers carry the candlestick from the Temple of Jerusalem in triumph.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: ...AD DECLARANDUM QUANTAE ALTITUDINIS MONS ET LOCUS TANTIS OPERIBUS SIT EGESTUS
The column is as tall as the hill that was dug away to make the Forum, the inscription says. The most beautiful letters ever cut in Rome.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: ...OB REM PUBLICAM RESTITUTAM IMPERIUMQUE POPULI ROMANI PROPAGATUM...

For the Republic restored and the Empire extended. Look closely at the fourth line: the name of his son Geta has been chiselled out, after his brother had him killed, and new words cut over the holes.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: INSTINCTU DIVINITATIS MENTIS MAGNITUDINE
By the prompting of the divinity and the greatness of his mind: which divinity, it does not say. Half the sculptures on it were taken from older monuments, emperors' heads recut as Constantine.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: HIC CONGESTA IACET QUAERIS SI TURBA PIORUM
Here lies, if you seek them, a crowd of the holy. Pope Damasus's verses for the martyrs, cut by his calligrapher Filocalus in letters no one had seen before, with little curls.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: SENATUS POPULUSQUE ROMANUS INCENDIO CONSUMPTUM RESTITUIT
The Senate and People of Rome restored what fire had consumed. The columns they put back were odd ones, taken from other buildings.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: ROMA
Someone has scratched the word on a broken tile and propped it up against a column. That is all.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: STRANGER, WHAT I HAVE TO SAY IS SHORT: STAND AND READ IT. HERE IS THE UNLOVELY TOMB OF A LOVELY WOMAN. HER PARENTS NAMED HER CLAUDIA. SHE LOVED HER HUSBAND WITH HER HEART. SHE KEPT THE HOUSE. SHE WORKED THE WOOL. I HAVE SPOKEN. GO.
Tombs line the roads out of Rome, and they talk to you as you pass: stranger, stop, read. It is the only way the dead can go on being in company.

steps.end: You say the words over to yourself, the way Romans read: aloud.

steps.say: A heavy bronze as, cast in a mould, not struck, with a head on each side. It weighs as much as a small stone. Rome has only just begun to make money at all; your grandfather paid in lumps of bronze by weight.
A silver denarius, new since the war with Hannibal: helmeted Roma on the front and the Twins, Castor and Pollux, riding with their spears on the back. Nearly pure silver.
A denarius. The young moneyers put their own ancestors on it now, to advertise the family: a triumph, a temple, a famous great-grandfather. It is still good silver.

A brass sestertius of Antoninus: the Emperor's calm bearded head, and on the back a goddess with her attributes. The silver denarius beside it in your purse is about three parts silver in four, and falling.
A little bronze coin with the Emperor's head and a wash of silver that rubs off in a week. The gold solidus, seventy-two to the pound, is the only money anyone trusts. You have never held one.
A tiny bronze nummus, smaller than your fingernail, the Emperor's name round it and no one can read it. You need hundreds for a loaf.

A big copper follis of the Emperor Justinian, marked M: forty nummi. Beside it, a copper of the Goth king Totila, struck in Rome, with his name: BADUILA. Two kings in one purse, and neither buys bread.
